function: STAR-RIS amplitude and element-partitioning configuration with user power allocation, maximizing ergodic sum rate; a DNN approximates the ergodic rate inside PSO (ML-PSO) (p. 6-7).
system: Single-antenna HD APs (one transmits, one receives) and single-antenna users with best-user selection; N-element STAR-RIS (simultaneously transmitting and reflecting, mode switching); band not stated (p. 3-4).
method: Fully connected DNN (two hidden layers of 500 eLU neurons), supervised regression (MSE loss, Adam) of the ergodic rate; PSO optimizes over its predictions (p. 7).
data_channel: Synthetic: 50,000 samples from the analytical ergodic-rate expression (14) under generalized Nakagami-m fading with uniform phases, split 90%/10% for training/testing; Monte Carlo Nakagami-m simulation (p. 4, p. 7).
test_conditions: 90/10 train/test split of the same generated samples (input ranges unstated); ESR evaluated for 20-100 STAR-RIS elements with 1 or 2 users per side (p. 7, p. 11).
baselines: Non-learned: alternating optimization, conventional reflecting-only RIS, FPRTE (fixed parameters), exhaustive search, analytical-PSO; learned: only own DNN variants with other depth/width (p. 10-12).
metrics: Outage probability, system outage probability, ergodic rate, ergodic sum rate, convergence over PSO iterations, MSE of ergodic-rate prediction, average computation time (p. 8-12).
complexity: Measured average runtime, Table III: ML-PSO 2.95 s versus AO 3.31 s and analytical-PSO 179-357 s, Xeon CPU; weight matrices 22x500, 500x500, 500x1 (p. 8, p. 11).
q1_support: p. 4: "|hpq| ∼ Nak (mpq, ḡpq)", with Nak defined in Table II as "Generalized Nakagami-m fading distribution"; p. 7: "we generate a dataset comprising 50,000 samples by computing (14)". Custom Nakagami-m simulator; no 3GPP, COST 2100, DeepMIMO, or measured channel.
q2_support: p. 7: "90% of the data is allocated for training the DNN model, while the remaining 10% is reserved for testing purposes". Only a held-out part of the same generated data; input ranges are not stated and no test on conditions excluded from training is reported.
q3_support: p. 11: "We compare its performance with the AO, the conventional-RIS and the FPRTE scheme." All non-learned (also exhaustive search and analytical-PSO). The only learned comparisons are variants of its own DNN, p. 12: "in comparison to models with H = 2 (Nh = 100) and H = 1 (Nh = 500)", which do not count.
q4_support: p. 11: "this comes at a greater computational cost (3.31 seconds) compared to JPRTE (which takes 2.95 seconds)"; Table III reports measured average computation times of the proposed ML-PSO.
q5_support: p. 7: "we generate a dataset comprising 50,000 samples by computing (14) with varying input values". Data are synthetic from the paper's own expression; no code or data link and no public channel dataset anywhere in the paper.
notes: PDF matches the DOI (title and DOI on p. 1). Borderline eligibility for the reviewer: the learned component is a supervised DNN that approximates the paper's analytical ergodic-rate expression (14), and PSO, a non-learned metaheuristic, chooses the STAR-RIS amplitudes, element partitioning, and power allocations from the DNN predictions (ML-PSO, p. 7-8). I included it because the DNN is an integral part of the proposed solution, as in deep unfolding, rather than motivation, a baseline, or the application; a surrogate inside a classical optimizer could instead be judged no_learning (p. 7). The JPRTE-SOP solution is plain PSO, and the STAR-RIS phases follow coherent combining with instantaneous CSI, neither learned (p. 3, p. 5). Area 3: the learned method configures the STAR-RIS (amplitudes, element partitioning) jointly with power allocation, with ergodic sum rate as its metric (p. 11). APs and users are single-antenna (p. 4, footnote 2), but the STAR-RIS makes the system check pass. No carrier frequency is stated.
